description: TUnit-native fluent time-assertion DSL on FakeTimeProvider plus assertion-level timing budget chain extensions via [AssertionExtension]. Provides Assert.That(fakeTime).HasAdvancedExactly(...) / HasAdvancedApproximately(...) / HasUtcNow(...) / HasUtcNowApproximately(...), Assert.That(timestamp).IsRecent(...) / IsBeforeNow(...) / IsAfterNow(...), the cross-cutting Assert.That(value).IsX().And.WithinTimeBudget(TimeSpan) / WithinTimeBudgetCapturing(TimeSpan, Action<TimeSpan>) on any TUnit assertion chain, and timer assertions on an ObservableTimeProvider: leaks (HasNoActiveTimers), fires (HasTimerFiredCount), schedules (HasTimerScheduled), and event-driven waits (HasNoActiveTimersEventually, HasTimerScheduledEventually) that react to each timer change instead of polling. Composes with sibling assertion packages without a binary dependency. AOT-compatible, trimmable, no reflection.
releaseNotes:
View the rendered release notes: https://github.com/JohnVerheij/TimeAssertions.TUnit/releases/tag/v0.10.0

Minor release. The "eventually" timer assertions now react to each timer change instead of polling, the core gains awaitable timer events and an `ObservableFakeTimeProvider` that advances without real time, and new assertions find a timer by its due time. The `pollingInterval` overloads are deprecated (see Upgrade).

### Added

- **`ObservableFakeTimeProvider`** is an `ObservableTimeProvider` over its own `FakeTimeProvider`: one object to inject into the code under test, to advance (`Advance`, `SetUtcNow`), and to assert on. `Fake` exposes the owned `FakeTimeProvider` for its other settings.
- **`ObservableFakeTimeProvider.AdvanceAndSettleAsync(TimeSpan delta, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`** advances the fake clock and then waits until every loop woken by the advance has armed its next wait (as many timers created with a finite due time or re-scheduled with `Change` as one-shot timers fired), so the next assertion sees the loop's step completed without a real-time sleep. The counts are those of the whole provider, so it suits loops that are the only code arming timers on it. A loop that ends after its timer fired makes the wait run until the token is canceled; the `OperationCanceledException` then says how many timers fired and how many were armed.
- **`ObservableFakeTimeProvider.AdvanceOnEachTimerUntilAsync(Task until, TimeSpan step, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`** advances by `step` each time the code under test has created a timer, until `until` completes: it drives a reconnect backoff with any number of failed attempts. It counts every timer created on the provider, so it suits a provider the loop has to itself, and `step` must cover the loop's longest single wait.
- **`ObservableFakeTimeProvider.AdvanceUntilAsync(TimeSpan step, Func<bool> until, TimeSpan maxAdvance, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`** advances in settled steps until `until` holds, for loops driven by a periodic timer (for example "until `TimerFireCount` reaches 6"). It throws `TimeoutException` after `maxAdvance` of fake time (the last step is shortened so the clock never passes it), so the outcome is deterministic.
- **`ObservableTimeProvider.TimersCreatedCount`** and **`TimersDisposedCount`** count every timer created and disposed through the provider. Unlike `ActiveTimerCount`, they never go down, so "has the loop armed its second backoff" can be answered when the loop is the only code creating timers on the provider.
- **`ObservableTimeProvider.WaitUntilAsync(Func<ObservableTimeProvider, bool> condition, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`** waits until the condition holds, re-checking it each time a timer is created, re-scheduled, fired, or disposed. No polling and no real-time delay; the token is the bound.
- **`ObservableTimeProvider.WaitForTimersCreatedAsync(long count, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`** and **`WaitForTimersDisposedAsync(long count, CancellationToken cancellationToken)`** wait for the creation and disposal counts. A creation is signaled only once the inner provider has scheduled the timer, so an advance right after the wait is never too early for it.
- **`Assert.That(time).HasTimerScheduled(TimeSpan dueTime, int atLeast = 1)`** asserts that at least `atLeast` active timers carry `dueTime`, among any number of loops; `HasNextTimerDueApproximately` only sees the earliest timer.
- **`Assert.That(time).HasNoTimerScheduled()`** asserts that no active timer has a pending due time. An undisposed but disabled timer passes, unlike with `HasNoActiveTimers()`.
- **`Assert.That(time).HasTimerScheduledEventually(TimeSpan dueTime, ...)`** waits until a timer, or at least `atLeast` timers, carry `dueTime`, for example until both ping loops have armed their delay. Forms: `(dueTime, cancellationToken)`, `(dueTime, timeout, cancellationToken)`, `(dueTime, atLeast, cancellationToken)`, and `(dueTime, atLeast, timeout, cancellationToken)`.
- **`HasNoActiveTimersEventually(CancellationToken)`**, **`HasActiveTimersEventually(CancellationToken)`**, **`HasActiveTimerCountEventually(int, CancellationToken)`**, **`HasAtLeastActiveTimerCountEventually(int, CancellationToken)`**, and **`HasAtMostActiveTimerCountEventually(int, CancellationToken)`** wait bounded by the token only, typically the test's own.
- **`TimeRenderingHelpers.FormatScheduledTimerShortfall`** and **`FormatUnexpectedScheduledTimers`** render the failure messages of the due-time assertions.

### Changed

- **BREAKING:** binary only: assemblies compiled against 0.9.0 must be rebuilt. **`ObservableTimeProvider`** is no longer `sealed`, and its `TimeProvider` overrides are; every timer assertion now applies to a derived provider such as `ObservableFakeTimeProvider`, because the generated assertion extensions are generic over the provider type. Source that calls the assertions compiles unchanged, including the deprecated `pollingInterval` forms, which `EventuallyTimerAssertionExtensions` now declares; code compiled against 0.9.0 still calls the old non-generic extension methods and fails with `MissingMethodException` until it is rebuilt.
- **`HasNoActiveTimersEventually`**, **`HasActiveTimersEventually`**, **`HasActiveTimerCountEventually`**, **`HasAtLeastActiveTimerCountEventually`**, and **`HasAtMostActiveTimerCountEventually`** no longer poll every 10 ms: they re-check the active count each time a timer changes, so a disposal is seen when it happens. The `timeout` is still a real-time bound, and the outcome of every assertion is unchanged.
- **`ObservableTimeProvider`** publishes a timer's new schedule (`ActiveTimers`, `NextTimerDueTime`) only once the inner timer has applied the change, so a test that sees the new schedule and then advances the fake clock fires the timer. A change that the inner timer rejects (it throws, or returns `false` as for a disposed timer) now leaves the previous schedule in place, and `AdvanceAndSettleAsync` does not count it as an armed wait. When a callback changes its timer again while a change fires it (run now, then again later), the schedule of that later change is published, as the inner timer carries it. `Change` calls on one timer from several threads are applied one at a time, so the published schedule is always the one the inner timer applied last; a callback that the inner provider fires during a `Change` runs once that change is applied, before `Change` returns. If such callbacks throw, all of them still run and `Change` throws (one exception as it was thrown, several as an `AggregateException`); an exception from the inner timer's `Change` takes precedence.
- **`TimeAssertions`** (the core package) now depends on `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` 10.11.0 for `ObservableFakeTimeProvider`. `TimeAssertions.TUnit` already depended on it, so a TUnit consumer gets no new package.
- **`TUnit.Assertions`** and **`TUnit.Core`** minimum versions raised from 1.53.0 to 1.77.0, and **`Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing`** from 10.7.0 to 10.11.0.

### Deprecated

- **`HasNoActiveTimersEventually(timeout, pollingInterval, ...)`**, **`HasActiveTimersEventually(timeout, pollingInterval, ...)`**, **`HasActiveTimerCountEventually(count, timeout, pollingInterval, ...)`**, **`HasAtLeastActiveTimerCountEventually(count, timeout, pollingInterval, ...)`**, and **`HasAtMostActiveTimerCountEventually(count, timeout, pollingInterval, ...)`** are `[Obsolete]`: the wait no longer polls, so `pollingInterval` has no effect. They forward to the forms without it and will be removed in 0.11.0. A build that treats warnings as errors fails on them until the argument is removed. A non-positive `pollingInterval` no longer throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. They keep source compatibility only: callers compiled against 0.9.0 need a rebuild (see Changed).

### Removed

- **BREAKING:** the five `*EventuallyAssertion` classes lost their constructors with a `pollingInterval` parameter, replaced by `(context, [count,] timeout, cancellationToken = default)` and `(context, [count,] cancellationToken)`. Only code that constructs these classes directly is affected; calls through `Assert.That(...)` are not.
- **BREAKING:** `EventuallyTimerAssertionExtensions` no longer declares the `(timeout, cancellationToken)` and `(count, timeout, cancellationToken)` overloads added in 0.8.0; the generated extensions take the same arguments. Only a call through the class name (`EventuallyTimerAssertionExtensions.HasNoActiveTimersEventually(...)`) is affected.

### Fixed

- **`ObservableTimeProvider`** documentation said that an inner provider never fires a timer while creating it. A `FakeTimeProvider` fires a timer that is due at once (a zero due time) during `CreateTimer`; the provider counts that fire correctly, and the documentation now says so.

**Upgrade:** remove the `pollingInterval` argument from the "eventually" timer assertions: `HasNoActiveTimersEventually(timeout, pollingInterval, ct)` becomes `HasNoActiveTimersEventually(timeout, ct)`, or `HasNoActiveTimersEventually(ct)` to wait as long as the test's token allows. To stop holding two objects, replace `new ObservableTimeProvider(fakeTime)` plus `fakeTime.Advance(...)` with one `ObservableFakeTimeProvider`.
